claude-s · story-video

A founder story in 27 seconds

1854: John Snow and the Broad Street pump

Make a 35-second vertical story video of a true story: London 1854, John Snow and the Broad Street pump, how plotting where the cholera deaths happened led him to the source. Every fact has to be right, and it should look like it was printed in 1854, not like a startup ad.

What the skill did

  • True story, checked against Snow's own book (On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 1855) and the HistData digitisation of his map. It claims nothing the sources don't support: it never says the handle ended the outbreak, which Snow himself wrote was already waning.
  • Designed as an 1854 broadside: Clarendon, Caslon and Baskerville italic on rag paper, with every line set to fill the measure. One Prussian blue is used for one thing only, water.
  • 18 cards, one per spoken phrase, each cut 50 ms before its line. Every word prints in on the frame it is spoken, using faster-whisper word times on each Chatterbox take.
  • The cold open prints Snow's own daily death counts as black bars (515 in ten days) while the dateline ticks from 31 August to 9 September. The map then draws itself from his 578 recorded deaths, closing in on the pump.
  • The pump's handle is drawn as its own piece and falls off on the word 'off'. The last card is the memorial pump in Soho, which has no handle.
  • Two critique rounds: hook 5 to 7 (a cold open on the count), voice 5 to 7 (re-narrated slower; 7 garbled takes caught and re-rolled), pacing 6 to 7.5 (a longer map moment). 1080x1920, 34.8 s. Portrait: John Snow, 1856, public domain.

Sound

  • A sub on every hard cut, one tick per day on the cold open, and a pen scratch as the map inks in.
  • An Am-F-Dm-E arp under the voice drops into a slow four-on-the-floor on 'the pump on Broad Street'. The beat is the pump: it stops dead with a cast-iron clank on 'comes off', and the handle lands off-screen.
  • The music ducks 12 dB under the voice. 0.5 s of true silence comes before the end card, then the last note echoes out. -14.0 LUFS, -1.4 dBTP.
27 second founder story: Amara, an ICU nurse in Leeds, wasted hours texting to swap shifts, learned to code on her breaks, two apps flopped, then she shipped Nightrota and 40 hospitals use it. End card nightrota.app. (Fictional brand and person, invent the details.)

What the skill did

  • Fictional: Amara, Nightrota, the doctor, the hospitals and every number are invented for this demo. No real person or brand.
  • 19 title cards, one per spoken phrase, narrated locally with Chatterbox. Each card lasts as long as its line, and the cut lands 50 ms before the word.
  • Every take was transcribed with faster-whisper and checked against the script. 5 of the 19 first takes were garbled or wrong and were re-rolled or rephrased (an invented brand name is spelled the way it sounds).
  • Text cards crossfade over 2 frames. Hard cuts are kept for the photos, the white contrast beats, the 'why not just ship it?' drop and the end card.
  • Photos settle in with an exponential zoom (1.12 to 1.0, time constant 0.4 s), rendered as float crop boxes in PIL rather than ffmpeg zoompan, which jitters.
  • Rendered at 4K 29.97 fps in about 25 s; this page embeds a 720p copy.
  • Photo credits, all CC0 Unsplash photos via Wikimedia Commons: 'Person sitting in hallway' by PICSELI; 'Macro laptop coding' by Marc Mueller; 'Vietnam woman on smartphone' by Tony Lam Hoang.

Sound

  • The music ducks 12 dB under the voice while it speaks and comes back up in pauses longer than 0.3 s (the shared sfx.py engine).
  • Only hard cuts get a sound: a sub boom with a passby peaking 50 ms before the cut on photos and the drop, and a sub on the payoff and the end card. Crossfaded text cards stay quiet.
  • The bed is a 16th-note arp about 17 dB under the voice until the drop, then four-on-the-floor about 10 dB under. Its tempo is fitted so the drop lands on a bar line.
  • There is true silence before 'Forty hospitals run on it today' (0.4 s) and before the end card (0.45 s), measured at -92 and -96 dBFS.
  • No stinger at the end: the bed stops on the end card and its last note echoes out on dotted eighths, each repeat quieter and darker.
